query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-oxidizing FeNiCrCoCu coatings to form a thin, nanocrystalline, and adherent oxide layer will reduce microscopic plastic deformation and overall wear during high-temperature sliding (above 400°C) by acting as both a thermal barrier and a mechanical impediment to dislocation nucleation compared with the as‐deposited state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (adjusting temperature and duration to tailor oxide layer thickness and uniformity) to deliberately form a continuous nanocrystalline oxide layer on the coating surface
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding tests under atmospheric conditions at temperatures above 400°C where oxidation kinetics and thermally activated deformation mechanisms are significant
generation.structural_mediator: A pre-formed, nanocrystalline, adherent oxide layer covering the alloy surface
generation.mechanism: The protective oxide layer acts as a barrier that impedes dislocation nucleation and limits the direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding, reducing localized plastic deformation and wear. Its presence also provides thermal stability that mitigates softening of the underlying microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings that undergo pre-oxidation will exhibit lower wear rates and reduced microscopic plastic deformation (observable via lower dislocation densities and smoother wear tracks) relative to as-deposited coatings when tested under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without a pre-formed oxide layer
generation.boundary: This effect is predicted to hold under high-temperature (T > 400°C) sliding in an atmospheric environment; deviations from these conditions, such as inert atmospheres or lower temperatures, could lead to different oxidation behaviors and mechanical responses.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal oxide layer thickness, uniformity, and the precise quantitative reductions in wear and deformation remain to be fully determined. It is also uncertain how variations in sliding speed and load might modulate the effectiveness of the pre-formed oxide layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical metal substrates: one set in the as-deposited state and the other subjected to a controlled pre-oxidation treatment designed to produce a nanocrystalline oxide layer. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests (e.g., at temperatures exceeding 400°C) under the same load, speed, and duration. Characterize the oxide layer formation using SEM/TEM and measure wear performance and microscopic deformation via wear track analysis, friction measurements, and dislocation density assessments.
measurements: Dislocation density and plastic deformation features (using TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear volume and microscopic plastic deformation compared to the as-deposited coatings, or if a continuous and adherent oxide layer cannot be verified on the pre-treated samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. decision.trend: Earlier studies on high-entropy alloy coatings under elevated temperatures have shown that wear resistance improves when a protective oxide layer forms during sliding. For example, work on AlCoCrFeNiTi HEA coatings (PMC7515071) demonstrated that at high temperatures a spinel phase develops on the wear track, reducing wear depth and friction. Subsequent studies (PMC9026100) exploited processing methods that refine the grain size and increase surface energy to accelerate the formation of adherent oxide layers. However, although these works indicate that oxidation and microstructural tailoring (via grain boundaries acting as rapid diffusion paths) correlate with improved tribological performance, no study has yet isolated the effect of a deliberately pre-induced oxide layer versus the as-deposited state in a controlled manner.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether the enhanced wear resistance and reduced microscopic plastic deformation under high-temperature sliding in FeNiCrCoCu coatings are governed primarily by the kinetics of forming a continuous, protective oxide layer at the surface or by changes in the underlying grain boundary mediated deformation. In other words, the causal role of pre-determined oxidation in arresting dislocation motion and controlling wear is an open question.
decision.lever: Implement a pre-oxidation treatment on FeNiCrCoCu coatings (varying the temperature and duration to control oxide layer thickness and uniformity) relative to the baseline as-deposited condition
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of using controlled processing modifications to decouple oxidation effects from other microstructural factors. By deliberately inducing a nanocrystalline, adherent oxide layer before sliding tests at temperatures >400°C, the experiment can directly test if this layer reduces wear rate and limits microscopic deformation (e.g., by inhibiting dislocation nucleation). A failure of wear resistance or a similar deformation mode in the pre-oxidized versus baseline coating would falsify this mechanistic hypothesis.
